hypergraph.source_text: Whilst I thus wished to think that all was false, it was absolutely necessary that I, who thus thought, should be somewhat; and as I observed that this truth, I think, therefore I am, was so certain and of such evidence that no ground of doubt, however extravagant, could be alleged by the sceptics capable of shaking it, I concluded that I might, without scruple, accept it as the first principle of the philosophy of which I was in search.

nodes.proposition: Even in radical doubt, the act of thinking or doubting is occurring.

span.verbatim_quote: Whilst I thus wished to think that all was false

nodes.speaker: Descartes

nodes.proposition: Whatever is actively thinking must exist while it is thinking.
nodes.speaker: Descartes (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: The thinker must exist as something while doubting.

span.verbatim_quote: it was absolutely necessary that I, who thus thought, should be somewhat

nodes.speaker: Descartes

nodes.proposition: Not even the most extravagant sceptical hypothesis can falsify the existence of the thinking subject in the moment of thought.

span.verbatim_quote: no ground of doubt, however extravagant, could be alleged by the sceptics capable of shaking it

nodes.speaker: Descartes

nodes.proposition: A proposition that survives maximal hyperbolic doubt qualifies as the foundational first principle of philosophy.
nodes.speaker: Descartes (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: I think, therefore I exist as the foundational first principle of philosophy.

span.verbatim_quote: I think, therefore I am

nodes.speaker: Descartes

hypergraph.source_text: All inferences from experience, therefore, are effects of custom, not of reasoning. For whenever the repetition of any particular act or operation produces a propensity to renew the same act or operation, without being impelled by any reasoning or process of the understanding, we always say, that this propensity is the effect of Custom.

nodes.proposition: Repeating an observation produces a psychological propensity to expect the same outcome without any demonstrative or probable reasoning step.

span.verbatim_quote: the repetition of any particular act or operation produces a propensity to renew the same act or operation, without being impelled by any reasoning or process of the understanding

nodes.speaker: David Hume

nodes.proposition: Any propensity formed by repetition without demonstrative or probable reasoning is by definition Custom (habit).

span.verbatim_quote: this propensity is the effect of Custom

nodes.speaker: David Hume

nodes.proposition: There is no non-circular Principle of the Uniformity of Nature capable of deductively justifying future expectations from past observations.
nodes.speaker: David Hume (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: All inductive inferences from past experience are effects of custom rather than rational demonstration.

span.verbatim_quote: All inferences from experience, therefore, are effects of custom, not of reasoning.

nodes.speaker: David Hume

hypergraph.source_text: And if the sufferings of children go to swell the sum of sufferings which was necessary to pay for truth, then I protest that the truth is not worth such a price. I would rather remain with my unavenged suffering and unsatisfied indignation, even if I were wrong. Too high a price is asked for harmony; it is beyond our means to pay so much to enter on it. And so I hasten to give back my entrance ticket.

nodes.proposition: Suppose eternal cosmic harmony requires the uncompensated torture and suffering of innocent children as a necessary means.

span.verbatim_quote: the sufferings of children go to swell the sum of sufferings which was necessary to pay for truth

nodes.speaker: Ivan Karamazov

nodes.proposition: No teleological or utilitarian future good can morally justify using the unredeemed suffering of an innocent child as an instrument (deontological side-constraint).
nodes.speaker: Ivan Karamazov (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Ultimate truth and eschatological harmony are morally unworthy of being purchased at the price of innocent children suffering.

span.verbatim_quote: the truth is not worth such a price

nodes.speaker: Ivan Karamazov

nodes.proposition: The moral cost of participating in such a cosmic harmony exceeds what conscience can legitimately pay.

span.verbatim_quote: Too high a price is asked for harmony; it is beyond our means to pay so much to enter on it.

nodes.speaker: Ivan Karamazov

nodes.proposition: If accepting a cosmic order requires consenting to an immoral price, a moral agent must refuse participation in that order even if the order is metaphysically real.
nodes.speaker: Ivan Karamazov (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Therefore, I morally refuse to accept the cosmic harmony and return my entrance ticket.

span.verbatim_quote: And so I hasten to give back my entrance ticket.

nodes.speaker: Ivan Karamazov

hypergraph.source_text: Piety, then, is that which is dear to the gods, and impiety is that which is not dear to them. The point which I should first wish to understand is whether the pious or holy is beloved by the gods because it is holy, or holy because it is beloved of the gods. But that which is dear to the gods is dear to them because it is loved by them, not loved by them because it is dear to them.

nodes.proposition: Piety is identical with whatever is dear to (beloved by) the gods.

span.verbatim_quote: Piety, then, is that which is dear to the gods

nodes.speaker: Euthyphro

nodes.proposition: Being loved by the gods is what causally and constitutively makes an action holy.
nodes.speaker: Euthyphro (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Something is holy because it is beloved of the gods.

span.verbatim_quote: holy because it is beloved of the gods

nodes.speaker: Euthyphro

nodes.proposition: The pious or holy is beloved by the gods because it is already holy.

span.verbatim_quote: the pious or holy is beloved by the gods because it is holy

nodes.speaker: Socrates

nodes.proposition: Being god-beloved (dear to the gods) is a passive state explained by the gods loving it.

span.verbatim_quote: that which is dear to the gods is dear to them because it is loved by them

nodes.speaker: Socrates

nodes.proposition: Two properties whose causal-explanatory ordering runs in opposite directions cannot be identical.
nodes.speaker: Socrates (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: God-belovedness is not the explanatory essence of holiness, since holiness is not caused merely by being dear to the gods.

span.verbatim_quote: not loved by them because it is dear to them

nodes.speaker: Socrates

hypergraph.source_text: Thesis: Causality in accordance with laws of nature is not the only causality from which the appearances of the world can one and all be derived. To explain these appearances it is necessary to assume that there is also another causality, that of freedom. Let us assume that there is no other kind of causality than that in accordance with laws of nature. Antithesis: There is no freedom; everything in the world takes place solely in accordance with laws of nature.

nodes.proposition: Suppose every event has a prior natural cause ad infinitum, yielding no unconditioned first beginning.

span.verbatim_quote: Let us assume that there is no other kind of causality than that in accordance with laws of nature.

nodes.speaker: Kant (Thesis Proof)

nodes.proposition: An infinite regress of dependent conditions fails to provide a complete sufficient explanation of phenomena.
nodes.speaker: Kant (Thesis Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Causality through transcendental freedom is necessary alongside the laws of nature.

span.verbatim_quote: To explain these appearances it is necessary to assume that there is also another causality, that of freedom.

nodes.speaker: Kant (Dogmatic Thesis)

nodes.proposition: Every empirical event in time must conform to an unbroken causal rule connecting it to a preceding state.

span.verbatim_quote: laws of nature

nodes.speaker: Kant (Antithesis Proof)

nodes.proposition: An uncaused spontaneous beginning would violate the causal unity required for coherent empirical experience.
nodes.speaker: Kant (Antithesis Implicit)

nodes.proposition: There is no freedom; everything in the world occurs solely by laws of nature.

span.verbatim_quote: There is no freedom; everything in the world takes place solely in accordance with laws of nature.

nodes.speaker: Kant (Empiricist Antithesis)

hypergraph.source_text: First, if any opinion is compelled to silence, that opinion may, for aught we can certainly know, be true. To deny this is to assume our own infallibility. It is not the feeling sure of a doctrine (be it what it may) which I call an assumption of infallibility. It is the undertaking to decide that question for others, without allowing them to hear what can be said on the contrary side.

nodes.proposition: Holding a strong personal conviction that a doctrine is true does not presume infallibility.

span.verbatim_quote: It is not the feeling sure of a doctrine (be it what it may) which I call an assumption of infallibility.

nodes.speaker: Censor

nodes.proposition: If a doctrine is earnestly felt to be certain, authorities are entitled to enforce it by silencing dissent.
nodes.speaker: Censor (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Authorities may legitimately decide truth for others by silencing contrary opinions.

span.verbatim_quote: the undertaking to decide that question for others, without allowing them to hear what can be said on the contrary side.

nodes.speaker: Censor

nodes.proposition: Any suppressed opinion might in fact be true given human fallibility.

span.verbatim_quote: if any opinion is compelled to silence, that opinion may, for aught we can certainly know, be true.

nodes.speaker: J.S. Mill

nodes.proposition: No human authority possesses epistemic infallibility, and acting as if infallible is epistemically illegitimate.
nodes.speaker: J.S. Mill (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Denying the fallibility of silencing dissent assumes unjustified human infallibility and is illegitimate.

span.verbatim_quote: To deny this is to assume our own infallibility.

nodes.speaker: J.S. Mill

hypergraph.source_text: And assuredly that, than which nothing greater can be conceived, cannot exist in the understanding alone. For, suppose it exists in the understanding alone: then it can be conceived to exist in reality; which is greater. You could no more doubt that this island which is more excellent than all lands exists somewhere in reality than you can doubt that that is in your understanding.

nodes.proposition: Suppose that than which nothing greater can be conceived exists in the understanding alone.

span.verbatim_quote: suppose it exists in the understanding alone

nodes.speaker: St. Anselm

nodes.proposition: Existing in reality as well as in the understanding is greater than existing in the understanding alone.

span.verbatim_quote: it can be conceived to exist in reality; which is greater

nodes.speaker: St. Anselm

nodes.proposition: Extramental existence is a genuine perfection-making property that increases a being's greatness.
nodes.speaker: St. Anselm (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: That than which nothing greater can be conceived cannot exist in the understanding alone, and therefore exists in reality.

span.verbatim_quote: that, than which nothing greater can be conceived, cannot exist in the understanding alone

nodes.speaker: St. Anselm

nodes.proposition: Any deductive schema that derives real existence from maximal conceptual excellence overgenerates absurd existent objects.
nodes.speaker: Gaunilo of Marmoutiers (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: By parallel reasoning, an unrealized lost island more excellent than all lands would have to exist in reality.

span.verbatim_quote: this island which is more excellent than all lands exists somewhere in reality

nodes.speaker: Gaunilo of Marmoutiers

hypergraph.source_text: God is a substance consisting of infinite attributes, of which each expresses eternal and infinite essentiality, and God necessarily exists; therefore if any substance besides God were granted, it would have to be explained by some attribute of God, and thus two substances with the same attribute would exist, which is absurd; therefore no substance can exist, or be conceived, besides God.

nodes.proposition: God necessarily exists as a substance consisting of infinite attributes, each expressing eternal infinite essence.

span.verbatim_quote: God is a substance consisting of infinite attributes, of which each expresses eternal and infinite essentiality, and God necessarily exists

nodes.speaker: Baruch Spinoza

nodes.proposition: Suppose a second substance besides God is granted, which must then be conceived through one of God's attributes.

span.verbatim_quote: if any substance besides God were granted, it would have to be explained by some attribute of God

nodes.speaker: Baruch Spinoza

nodes.proposition: Two distinct substances cannot share the exact same attribute in nature (Ethics I, Prop. 5).
nodes.speaker: Baruch Spinoza (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Positing another substance entails the absurdity of two substances sharing the same attribute.

span.verbatim_quote: two substances with the same attribute would exist, which is absurd

nodes.speaker: Baruch Spinoza

nodes.proposition: Therefore no substance besides God can exist or be conceived.

span.verbatim_quote: no substance can exist, or be conceived, besides God

nodes.speaker: Baruch Spinoza

hypergraph.source_text: God is, or He is not. Reason can decide nothing here. A game is being played at the extremity of this infinite distance where heads or tails will turn up. Let us weigh the gain and the loss in wagering that God is. If you gain, you gain all; if you lose, you lose nothing. Wager, then, without hesitation that He is.

nodes.proposition: Theoretical reason alone cannot settle whether God exists.

span.verbatim_quote: Reason can decide nothing here.

nodes.speaker: Blaise Pascal

nodes.proposition: Human life forces an unavoidable practical choice equivalent to wagering on God's existence.

span.verbatim_quote: A game is being played at the extremity of this infinite distance where heads or tails will turn up.

nodes.speaker: Blaise Pascal

nodes.proposition: Wagering that God exists yields infinite gain if true and negligible finite loss if false.

span.verbatim_quote: If you gain, you gain all; if you lose, you lose nothing.

nodes.speaker: Blaise Pascal

nodes.proposition: The decision matrix contains only one coherent infinite-reward deity rather than rival mutually exclusive gods.
nodes.speaker: Blaise Pascal (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Rational agents facing forced epistemic uncertainty ought to choose the action with dominant expected value.
nodes.speaker: Blaise Pascal (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: One ought rationally to wager without hesitation that God exists.

span.verbatim_quote: Wager, then, without hesitation that He is.

nodes.speaker: Blaise Pascal

hypergraph.source_text: Have the carpenter, then, and the shoemaker certain functions and courses of action, and has man as man none, but is he born without a function? Life seems to be common even to plants, while we are seeking what is peculiar to man. There remains, then, an active life of the element that has a rational principle. Human good turns out to be activity of soul in accordance with virtue.

nodes.proposition: Just as artisans and bodily parts have characteristic functions, human beings qua human possess a distinctive function.

span.verbatim_quote: Have the carpenter, then, and the shoemaker certain functions and courses of action, and has man as man none, but is he born without a function?

nodes.speaker: Aristotle

nodes.proposition: Nutritive biological life is shared with plants and animals, so it cannot be what is distinctive to human beings.

span.verbatim_quote: Life seems to be common even to plants, while we are seeking what is peculiar to man.

nodes.speaker: Aristotle

nodes.proposition: Active exercise of the rational faculty remains as the distinctively human function.

span.verbatim_quote: There remains, then, an active life of the element that has a rational principle.

nodes.speaker: Aristotle

nodes.proposition: The supreme good of any natural kind consists in performing its characteristic species-function with excellence (virtue).
nodes.speaker: Aristotle (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: The supreme human good (eudaimonia) is activity of the soul in accordance with rational virtue.

span.verbatim_quote: Human good turns out to be activity of soul in accordance with virtue.

nodes.speaker: Aristotle

hypergraph.source_text: Epicurus's old questions are yet unanswered. Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is he impotent. Is he able, but not willing? then is he malevolent. Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?

nodes.proposition: A deity willing to prevent evil yet unable to do so lacks omnipotence.

span.verbatim_quote: Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is he impotent.

nodes.speaker: Philo (quoting Epicurus)

nodes.proposition: A deity able to prevent evil yet unwilling to do so lacks perfect benevolence.

span.verbatim_quote: Is he able, but not willing? then is he malevolent.

nodes.speaker: Philo (quoting Epicurus)

nodes.proposition: Genuine evil exists in the world without any morally overriding reason that compels an omnipotent benevolent deity to allow it.
nodes.speaker: Epicurus (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: The persistence of evil is incompatible with the simultaneous omnipotence and perfect benevolence of God.

span.verbatim_quote: Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?

nodes.speaker: Philo (quoting Epicurus)

hypergraph.source_text: See how the minnows are darting about! That is the pleasure of fishes. You not being a fish yourself, how can you possibly know in what consists the pleasure of fishes? You not being I, how can you know that I do not know? You asked me how I knew what made fishes happy, so you already knew that I knew when you asked me. I knew it from my own feelings on this bridge.

nodes.proposition: The minnows darting effortlessly through the stream display unforced natural vitality.

span.verbatim_quote: See how the minnows are darting about!

nodes.speaker: Zhuangzi

nodes.proposition: Zhuangzi directly perceives this attunement from his own lived experience standing on the Hao River bridge.

span.verbatim_quote: I knew it from my own feelings on this bridge.

nodes.speaker: Zhuangzi

nodes.proposition: Attuned perception across living beings can grasp creaturely flourishing without requiring species identity.
nodes.speaker: Zhuangzi (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: The darting minnows genuinely experience the joy of fishes.

span.verbatim_quote: That is the pleasure of fishes.

nodes.speaker: Zhuangzi

nodes.proposition: Because Zhuangzi is not a fish, he lacks epistemic access to what constitutes fish pleasure.

span.verbatim_quote: You not being a fish yourself, how can you possibly know in what consists the pleasure of fishes?

nodes.speaker: Huizi

nodes.proposition: By Huizi's own species-barrier principle, since Huizi is not Zhuangzi, Huizi cannot know what Zhuangzi fails to know.

span.verbatim_quote: You not being I, how can you know that I do not know?

nodes.speaker: Zhuangzi

nodes.proposition: Asking whence Zhuangzi knew what makes fishes happy grammatically presupposes that Zhuangzi did know.

span.verbatim_quote: You asked me how I knew what made fishes happy, so you already knew that I knew when you asked me.

nodes.speaker: Zhuangzi

lenses.title: Lichtenberg Grammatical Reading
lenses.description: Retains explicit spans while replacing Cartesian substance bridging with an implicit grammatical undercutter questioning the move from thought to an enduring 'I'.

hypergraph.source_text: Whilst I thus wished to think that all was false, it was absolutely necessary that I, who thus thought, should be somewhat; and as I observed that this truth, I think, therefore I am, was so certain and of such evidence that no ground of doubt, however extravagant, could be alleged by the sceptics capable of shaking it, I concluded that I might, without scruple, accept it as the first principle of the philosophy of which I was in search.

nodes.proposition: Whilst thinking or wishing to doubt occurs, mental activity is undeniable.

span.verbatim_quote: Whilst I thus wished to think that all was false

nodes.speaker: Descartes

nodes.proposition: Introspective awareness immediately attests only that thinking is taking place rather than proving an enduring metaphysical soul.
nodes.speaker: Lichtenberg (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Something thinking exists at the moment this doubt occurs.

span.verbatim_quote: it was absolutely necessary that I, who thus thought, should be somewhat

nodes.speaker: Descartes

nodes.proposition: Sceptical scenarios cannot overturn the certainty of present thinking.

span.verbatim_quote: no ground of doubt, however extravagant, could be alleged by the sceptics capable of shaking it

nodes.speaker: Descartes

nodes.proposition: Moving from "there is thinking" to a persistent substantial subject "I" commits a grammatical fallacy.
nodes.speaker: Lichtenberg Critique

nodes.proposition: The claim "I think, therefore I exist as an enduring thinking substance" serves as philosophy's first principle.

span.verbatim_quote: I think, therefore I am

nodes.speaker: Descartes

lenses.title: Teleological Theodicy Challenge
lenses.description: Omits Ivan's agent-consent enthymeme [E2] and introduces a teleological counter-premise rebutting the absolute deontological side-constraint.

hypergraph.source_text: And if the sufferings of children go to swell the sum of sufferings which was necessary to pay for truth, then I protest that the truth is not worth such a price. I would rather remain with my unavenged suffering and unsatisfied indignation, even if I were wrong. Too high a price is asked for harmony; it is beyond our means to pay so much to enter on it. And so I hasten to give back my entrance ticket.

span.verbatim_quote: the sufferings of children go to swell the sum of sufferings which was necessary to pay for truth

nodes.proposition: No future teleological good can justify using an innocent child's suffering as a mere instrument.

nodes.proposition: An infinite universal reconciliation can outweigh finite temporal suffering if free moral creatures choose redemption.
nodes.speaker: Teleological Theodicy (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Truth and eschatological harmony are not worth buying with children's suffering.

span.verbatim_quote: the truth is not worth such a price

nodes.proposition: Asking humanity to pay that price exceeds legitimate moral bounds.

span.verbatim_quote: Too high a price is asked for harmony; it is beyond our means to pay so much to enter on it.

lenses.description: Uses renamed proposition IDs (alt_*) and paraphrased voluntarist wording across all seven nodes to test semantic Hungarian bipartite node and undercutter alignment.

hypergraph.source_text: Piety, then, is that which is dear to the gods, and impiety is that which is not dear to them. nodes.proposition: Divine approval is what causes an act to be holy.
nodes.speaker: Euthyphro (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: An action is pious simply because it is beloved by the gods.

span.verbatim_quote: holy because it is beloved of the gods

nodes.speaker: Euthyphro

nodes.proposition: The gods love what is holy precisely because it already possesses holiness.

span.verbatim_quote: the pious or holy is beloved by the gods because it is holy

nodes.proposition: Being dear to the gods is an effect of their loving it.

span.verbatim_quote: that which is dear to the gods is dear to them because it is loved by them

nodes.speaker: Socrates

nodes.proposition: Two concepts with inverse explanatory order cannot be identical.
nodes.speaker: Socrates (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Being loved by the gods is only an accidental feature, not the essence of piety.

span.verbatim_quote: not loved by them because it is dear to them

nodes.speaker: Socrates

nodes.proposition: All appearances occur strictly according to laws of nature.

Let us weigh the gain and the loss in wagering that God is. If you gain, you gain all; if you lose, you lose nothing. Wager, then, without hesitation that He is.

nodes.proposition: Speculative reason alone cannot decide whether God exists.

span.verbatim_quote: Reason can decide nothing here.

nodes.speaker: Blaise Pascal

nodes.proposition: Life compels a practical choice concerning belief in God.

span.verbatim_quote: A game is being played at the extremity of this infinite distance where heads or tails will turn up.

nodes.proposition: Wagering on Pascal's God promises infinite reward if right and finite cost if wrong.

span.verbatim_quote: If you gain, you gain all; if you lose, you lose nothing.

nodes.speaker: Blaise Pascal

nodes.proposition: Only a single exclusive deity offers infinite reward in the decision table.

nodes.proposition: Rival possible deities with positive epistemic probability reward skepticism or punish wagering on competing gods, breaking expected-value dominance.
nodes.speaker: Denis Diderot (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Practical rationality under uncertainty maximizes expected utility.
nodes.speaker: Blaise Pascal (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: One ought rationally to wager without hesitation that Pascal's God exists.

span.verbatim_quote: Wager, then, without hesitation that He is.

lenses.title: Plantinga Free-Will Defense Reading
lenses.description: Introduces a libertarian free-will defense rebutting Epicurus's assumption [E1] that an omnipotent God can eliminate all moral evil without sacrificing genuine moral agency.

hypergraph.source_text: Epicurus's old questions are yet unanswered. Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is he impotent. Is he able, but not willing? then is he malevolent. Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?

nodes.proposition: A deity willing yet unable to prevent evil lacks omnipotence.

span.verbatim_quote: Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is he impotent.

nodes.speaker: Philo

nodes.proposition: A deity able yet unwilling to prevent evil lacks perfect goodness.

span.verbatim_quote: Is he able, but not willing? then is he malevolent.

nodes.speaker: Philo

nodes.proposition: An omnipotent benevolent God could prevent all evil without forfeiting any greater moral good.
nodes.speaker: Epicurus (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Creating significantly free moral agents is a supreme good that logically precludes causally guaranteeing they never choose evil.
nodes.speaker: Free-Will Defense (Implicit)

nodes.proposition: Evil proves God cannot be both omnipotent and wholly benevolent.

span.verbatim_quote: Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?

nodes.speaker: Philo
